finding.claim: SQL injection in /search: the q query parameter is interpolated directly into the SQL string via an f-string. An unauthenticated attacker can break out of the LIKE literal and run arbitrary SELECT logic, for example a UNION SELECT to read other tables (users, orders, sqlite_master) from shop.db.
finding.sink: db.execute(f"SELECT id, name FROM products WHERE name LIKE '%{term}%'") at app.py:12; results returned to the attacker via jsonify at app.py:13

trace.note: term = request.args.get('q', '') takes attacker-controlled input with no validation
term is formatted into the SQL text with an f-string, not bound as a parameter
fetched rows are serialized back in the response, so injected UNION results are exfiltrated directly

finding.guards_checked: No authentication or authorization on the route, no input validation or escaping, and no parameterized query. The other routes (app.py:18, app.py:25) use ? placeholders, but this one does not. No WAF or middleware exists in the file. sqlite3 execute() rejects multiple statements, so stacked queries are not possible, but UNION-based extraction still works. Example: /search?q=' UNION SELECT id, sql FROM sqlite_master--

verdict.reason: app.py:11 reads q from request.args with no validation, app.py:12 f-string-interpolates it into the SQL LIKE literal with no parameterization or auth, and app.py:13 returns the rows via jsonify, so UNION-based extraction works for an anonymous attacker.

verdict_facts.reason: app.py:11 reads q from request.args, app.py:12 puts it into the SQL text with an f-string, and app.py:13 returns the rows. The route has no auth decorator, validation or parameter binding, so an anonymous caller can run a UNION SELECT.
